history.content: Why did operating profit change from Q1 to Q2 2025? Identify the largest negative account contribution and investigate its monthly pattern.

Operating profit fell in Q2 versus Q1, driven primarily by higher COGS; the monthly pattern shows a sustained rise that accelerated in April and continued through June.
Operating profit decreased by $46,000 from Q1 to Q2. The accounting bridge attributes this to a $63,000 positive revenue contribution, offset by negative contributions of $83,000 from COGS and $26,000 from operating expenses; therefore, COGS was the largest negative account contribution.
COGS increased every month: $45,000 in January, $48,000 in February, $50,000 in March, $65,000 in April, $74,000 in May, and $87,000 in June. The largest month-over-month increase was $15,000 from March to April, followed by increases of $9,000 from April to May and $13,000 from May to June.
The data supports an accounting explanation—higher COGS was the main drag on Q2 operating profit—but does not identify the business cause of the COGS increase, such as supplier pricing, product mix, or volume.
The dataset contains financial aggregates only; it has no supplier, price, volume, product-mix, or staffing detail to establish why COGS rose.
The monthly pattern describes COGS levels and changes, not the underlying operational driver.
